question: The correct order of events in a four-stroke diesel engine is:
options: Intake, compression, power, exhaust
Intake, power, compression, exhaust
Compression, intake, exhaust, power, with the power stroke last
Power, intake, compression, exhaust
explanation: A four-stroke engine completes one working cycle every two crankshaft revolutions.

question: A two-stroke engine completes its working cycle in:
options: Half a crankshaft revolution
Four crankshaft revolutions
One crankshaft revolution
Two crankshaft revolutions
explanation: Scavenging and exhaust happen around bottom dead centre, so there is a power stroke every revolution.

question: Most modern large slow-speed two-stroke main engines use:
options: Four-stroke valve timing with inlet and exhaust cam followers
Uniflow scavenging with a cylinder head exhaust valve
Natural aspiration with no scavenge blowers or turbocharger
Loop scavenging with ports and no exhaust valve at all
explanation: Air enters through ports at the bottom of the liner and leaves through the exhaust valve at the top, giving efficient scavenging.

question: A diesel engine turbocharger turbine is driven by:
options: Exhaust gas
Gear drive from the crankshaft
Starting air
Electric motor
explanation: The turbine drives a compressor that supplies pressurised charge air, increasing power output.

question: In a crosshead engine, the crosshead allows:
options: The engine to run without cylinder lubrication for short periods
The piston to rotate freely in the liner, spreading the wear evenly around the bore
The fuel pump to change its timing as the engine load changes
The piston rod to move in a straight line, so a stuffing box can seal the crankcase
explanation: Side thrust is taken by the guides, and scavenge-space contamination is kept out of the crankcase oil.

question: The main purpose of a crankcase oil mist detector is to:
options: Monitor the exhaust smoke density at the funnel of the ship
Detect water in the fuel oil before it reaches the engine
Measure the viscosity of the lubricating oil in the sump and warn of dilution
Detect a rising oil mist level early to prevent a crankcase explosion
explanation: Oil mist forms at hot spots such as overheating bearings. On an alarm, slow down and stop, and do not open the crankcase until it has cooled.

question: Crankcase explosion relief valves are designed to:
options: Release lubricating oil from the sump when it becomes too hot, protecting the bearings
Relieve explosion pressure and stop flames leaving the crankcase
Admit fresh air into the crankcase to dilute the oil mist
Drain condensed water from the bottom of the sump tank
explanation: They are spring-loaded, self-closing and fitted with flame arresters, so a secondary explosion is less likely.

question: If fuel injection timing is too late, the likely result is:
options: No effect on the performance of the engine at normal load
Higher peak cylinder pressure and a lower exhaust temperature with less fuel burned
Lower peak cylinder pressure, higher exhaust temperature and fuel use
Faster engine starting and a lower fuel consumption at idle
explanation: Late injection makes combustion continue into the expansion stroke, sending more heat to the exhaust.

question: Typical signs of a scavenge fire include:
options: A drop in fuel oil viscosity and a rise in the lubricating oil pressure at the engine
Low cooling water temperature and low scavenge air pressure
High scavenge and exhaust temperatures and sparks from scavenge drains
Higher engine rpm with no change in the load or the fuel setting
explanation: Reduce speed, cut fuel to the unit, increase cylinder lubrication and use the fixed extinguishing system if the fire spreads.

question: Crankshaft deflection readings are taken to assess:
options: Fuel injector condition and the spray pattern of the nozzles
Turbocharger efficiency and the condition of the turbine blades
Piston ring wear and the condition of the cylinder liners
Main bearing alignment and wear
explanation: A dial gauge between the crank webs measures opening and closing as the crank turns. Excess deflection points to misalignment.

question: The main purpose of a charge air cooler is to:
options: Heat the air for easier starting of the engine in cold weather
Cool the lubricating oil leaving the main engine sump tank
Raise the density of the charge air so more oxygen enters
Clean the exhaust gas before it enters the turbocharger turbine
explanation: Cooler, denser air allows more fuel to be burned efficiently and lowers thermal load.

question: Typical main engine starting air receiver pressure is about:
options: 300 bar
30 bar
7 bar
3 bar
explanation: Receivers must hold enough air for a set number of consecutive starts (for example 12 for a reversible engine) without recharging.

question: A common cause of a starting air line explosion is:
options: A low fuel oil level in the service tank during manoeuvring
Low ambient temperature in the engine room at start-up
A leaking starting valve passing hot gas to an oily line
Too much cooling water entering the starting air receiver
explanation: Prevent it by draining the lines, keeping oil out of the compressed air and maintaining start valves. Flame arresters or bursting discs are fitted.

question: The compression ratio of a diesel engine is:
options: Cylinder bore divided by the length of the piston stroke
Maximum cylinder pressure divided by the pressure of the atmospheric air
The volume of fuel injected divided by the volume of air
Total cylinder volume at BDC divided by clearance volume at TDC
explanation: A high compression ratio gives the temperature needed for compression ignition.

question: The main function of an engine governor is to:
options: Measure the fuel consumption and send it to the bridge computer
Start the engine automatically when the standby generator is needed
Keep engine speed steady as load changes by adjusting the fuel
Control the cooling water temperature by operating the thermostat
explanation: It also provides overspeed protection together with a separate overspeed trip.

question: Fuel in a diesel engine ignites because of:
options: The heat of compression
A spark plug
Exhaust gas heat
A glow plug at all loads
explanation: Air compressed to a high ratio becomes hot enough to ignite injected fuel.

question: How many crankshaft revolutions does each cylinder of a four-stroke engine need for one power stroke?
options: Half a revolution
Two
Four
One
explanation: Intake, compression, power and exhaust take two revolutions (720°) in a four-stroke engine.

question: A large slow-speed two-stroke main engine is usually connected to the propeller:
options: Directly through the shafting, with no reduction gearbox
By chain and sprocket drive with a flexible coupling
Through an electric motor and a frequency converter only
Through a high-ratio reduction gearbox and a clutch on the thrust shaft
explanation: Slow-speed engines run at propeller speed, typically around 60-130 rpm.

question: Medium-speed four-stroke diesel engines are most commonly used on merchant ships as:
options: Generator (auxiliary) engines, and sometimes geared main engines
Boiler feed pumps and fuel transfer pumps in the engine room and workshop
Steering gear pumps, driven directly from the engine shaft
Emergency air compressors and fire pumps only on large ships
explanation: Their compact size and higher speed suit alternator drives.

question: The main job of a fuel injector is to:
options: Cool the cylinder head by spraying the fuel onto the valve seats
Measure the fuel quantity remaining in the service tank
Heat the fuel to its flash point before it enters the cylinder
Atomise the fuel and spray it into the combustion chamber
explanation: Good atomisation and penetration are needed for complete combustion.

question: Piston rings mainly serve to:
options: Cool the exhaust gas as it leaves the cylinder through the valve
Seal the combustion gases and pass heat from the piston to the liner
Hold the piston firmly to the connecting rod at its small end bearing
Inject cylinder oil into the combustion space at each stroke
explanation: Worn or stuck rings cause blow-by, loss of compression and possible scavenge fires.

question: Heat from the main engine jacket cooling water is often used to:
options: Produce fresh water in the fresh water generator
Drive the turbocharger turbine in place of exhaust gas
Charge the ship's batteries through a heat exchanger
Heat the fuel oil storage tanks to a temperature of 150 °C
explanation: The low-pressure evaporator boils sea water at reduced temperature using jacket water heat.

question: The turning gear interlock on a main engine:
options: Stops the engine if the bridge telegraph moves from the ordered position
Starts the auxiliary blowers before the engine is turned on air
Locks the propeller shaft during sea trials and shaft alignment
Prevents the engine being started while the turning gear is engaged
explanation: Starting with the turning gear engaged could cause serious damage and injury.

question: The main thrust bearing:
options: Cools the stern tube bearing with a flow of sea water
Transmits the propeller thrust to the ship's hull
Lubricates the crossheads and the guide shoes of the engine
Supports the weight of the flywheel and of the crankshaft only
explanation: It is usually built into the aft end of a slow-speed engine's bedplate.

question: Black smoke from a diesel engine's exhaust usually indicates:
options: Too much cooling water leaking into the combustion space
Water in the lubricating oil, which burns in the cylinders as steam and vapour
Incomplete combustion, e.g. overload, poor atomisation or lack of air
Perfect combustion with the correct air to fuel ratio
explanation: Check injectors, turbocharger and air coolers, and the engine load.

question: Specific fuel oil consumption (SFOC) of a diesel engine is usually expressed in:
options: Grams per kilowatt-hour (g/kWh)
Litres per hour, measured at the fuel flow meter
Kilowatts per tonne of fuel, as shown on the data sheet
Tonnes per nautical mile, as shown in the voyage report
explanation: Large two-stroke engines have SFOC values of roughly 160-180 g/kWh.

question: Which fault will normally cause an automatic shutdown of a diesel generator engine?
options: A slightly high cooling water temperature alarm
A low level in the day tank alarm
A dirty air filter
Low lubricating oil pressure
explanation: Overspeed and very low lube oil pressure are typical shutdowns; other faults usually give alarms first.

question: Starting air receivers should be drained regularly to:
options: Cool the air
Remove accumulated water and oil
Test the safety valve
Reduce the air pressure for safety
explanation: Oil in the starting air system increases the risk of a starting air line explosion.

question: Before starting a main engine after maintenance, it is turned over with the indicator cocks open in order to:
options: Charge the starting air receivers to the working pressure of the engine
Check that no water, oil or fuel is lying in the cylinders
Warm up the engine and the lubricating oil in the system
Test the overspeed trip and the emergency shutdown
explanation: Liquid in a cylinder cannot be compressed and could cause serious damage if the engine were started on fuel.

question: On a crosshead two-stroke engine, cylinder lubrication is provided by:
options: Fuel oil acting as a lubricant on the liner surface
Splash from the crankcase, thrown up by the crankshaft and crank webs
Separate cylinder oil injected through the liner by lubricators
Grease applied by hand to the liner during each overhaul
explanation: The stuffing box keeps the cylinder and crankcase oils separate.

question: The jacket cooling water outlet temperature of a slow-speed main engine is typically kept at about:
explanation: Too cold a liner promotes cold corrosion; too hot reduces the oil film and can cause boiling.

question: Engine jacket cooling water is commonly treated with:
options: A nitrite-based corrosion inhibitor, with regular tests of its strength
Detergent, to remove oil from the water jackets and the cooler
Sea water, to reduce the formation of scale in the engine water jackets
Hydrazine only, as it is used in boilers and steam systems
explanation: Rising chlorides suggest sea water contamination, for example from a leaking cooler.

question: On a crosshead engine, main and crankpin bearings are lubricated by:
options: Cylinder oil supplied from the lubricators on the engine
System oil pumped from the sump tank through the engine
Grease applied by grease nipples at each main bearing
Fuel oil taken from the day tank and filtered at the engine
explanation: The system oil also cools the pistons on many engines, via telescopic pipes or the crosshead.

question: Heavy fuel oil is heated before injection mainly to:
options: Remove its sulphur by heating it in the settling tank
Raise its flash point to above 60 °C for safe handling
Lower its viscosity to the value the engine maker recommends
Increase its density to improve the combustion in the cylinder
explanation: A viscosity controller usually regulates the heater to give around 10-15 cSt at the injectors.

question: A viscosity controller in the fuel system:
options: Adjusts the fuel heater to keep viscosity at the pumps constant
Measures the fuel tank level and sends a signal to the transfer pump
Stops the engine automatically when the viscosity becomes too high
Mixes a small quantity of water into the fuel to lower viscosity
explanation: Controlling viscosity rather than temperature compensates for differences between bunker deliveries.

question: Catalytic fines (aluminium and silicon particles) in fuel oil mainly cause:
options: Cold corrosion of the cylinder liner surfaces
A lower fuel density and a lower calorific value
Excessive smoke at low load and during manoeuvring operations only
Abrasive wear of fuel pumps, injectors, rings and liners
explanation: Good settling, purifying and filtering remove most cat fines before the fuel reaches the engine.

question: Marine fuel quality specifications are set out in the standard:
options: ISO 9001
ISO 8217
explanation: It gives limits for properties such as viscosity, density, sulphur, water, cat fines and flash point.

question: Turbocharger surging is:
options: Normal operation of the turbocharger at full engine load
Overheating of the turbocharger bearings due to loss of oil
An unstable reversal of air flow through the compressor, often with a bang
A leak in the exhaust manifold of the engine, close to the turbine inlet
explanation: Causes include fouled turbines or nozzles, dirty air coolers, sudden load changes and damaged blading.

question: Auxiliary blowers on a two-stroke main engine run at low load because:
options: The turbocharger cannot supply enough scavenge air at low load
They drive the camshaft when the engine speed is low
They cool the exhaust valves at low load and during air starting
They pump cooling water to the charge air coolers
explanation: They start and stop automatically depending on the scavenge air pressure.

question: A direct-reversible two-stroke engine is reversed by:
options: Reversing the turbocharger so that it drives the engine astern
Changing injection and starting air timing to astern, then starting in reverse
Changing the pitch of the propeller blades while the engine runs
Engaging a reverse gearbox between the engine and the propeller shaft
explanation: On camshaft engines this is done by shifting cams or the camshaft; electronic engines change timing by software.

question: During air starting, the cylinder starting valves are opened in firing order by:
options: The turbocharger, which supplies the scavenge air
The starting air distributor
The governor, which controls the engine speed
The fuel pumps, which are driven by the camshaft
explanation: Air is admitted shortly after TDC on the power stroke to turn the engine until it fires on fuel.

question: An indicator diagram (pressure-volume) of a cylinder is used to:
options: Test the quality of the cooling water in the jacket system
Check the bearing clearances in the crankcase of the engine
Measure the fuel level in the service tank of the engine and the settling tank
Assess cylinder power and check compression and peak pressures
explanation: Electronic pressure analysers now do the same job and help balance the cylinders.

question: Main bearing shells on large diesel engines are commonly lined with:
options: Rubber, bonded to a steel backing for damping
Cast iron, bolted into the bedplate of the engine
White metal (tin-based bearing alloy)
Aluminium oxide ceramic, fitted in the form of thin liners
explanation: White metal is soft enough to embed small particles and conform to the journal.

question: On many two-stroke engines, the pistons are cooled by:
options: System oil supplied through telescopic pipes or the crosshead
Fuel oil circulated through the piston from the booster pump
Sea water supplied through the piston rod from the jacket system
Scavenge air only, blown over the piston crown by the blowers
explanation: Some older designs used water cooling; oil cooling avoids water leaks into the crankcase.

question: In an oil-lubricated stern tube, the aft seal prevents:
options: Sea water entering and oil leaking out into the sea
Air entering the engine through the shaft from the tunnel
Exhaust gas reaching the propeller from the stern of the ship
Fuel leaking into the shaft from the engine room bilge
explanation: Oil leakage from stern tube seals is a pollution concern; environmentally acceptable lubricants are required in some areas.

question: A 'barred speed range' marked on a main engine tachometer exists to:
options: Save fuel by keeping the engine away from its most efficient speed range
Avoid running continuously at speeds that cause harmful torsional vibration
Limit the bridge's control of the engine in restricted waters
Protect the boiler from overload when the main engine speed is low
explanation: The engine may pass quickly through the barred range but must not be operated within it.

question: Electronically controlled two-stroke engines (such as ME or RT-flex types) differ from conventional engines mainly because they:
options: Have no turbocharger because the cylinders are supercharged by blowers
Use petrol instead of fuel oil for ignition in the cylinders
Are four-stroke engines with camshaft driven fuel pumps
Have no camshaft; injection and valve timing are electronic
explanation: Timing can be optimised for each load, improving fuel consumption and emissions.

question: A higher exhaust temperature on one cylinder than on the others may be caused by:
options: A correctly adjusted fuel pump and a well maintained injector
A clean air cooler and a low scavenge air temperature
A faulty fuel injector or a leaking exhaust valve
Low jacket water salinity and a low cooling water temperature
explanation: Compare cylinder pressures and inspect the injector and valve to find the cause.

question: Lubricating oil being burned in the cylinders usually shows as:
options: No visible smoke at all
Pure white steam from the funnel
Thick black smoke from the funnel
Blue-grey exhaust smoke
explanation: Causes include worn rings or liners, excessive cylinder oil feed or leaking valve guide seals.

question: Fuel injectors are tested on a test rig for:
options: The colour of the nozzle tip after a period of operation
Electrical insulation of the injector solenoid and cable
Opening pressure, spray pattern and leakage (dribbling)
The water content of the fuel which is delivered to the nozzle
explanation: Faulty injectors cause poor combustion, deposits and high exhaust temperatures.

question: Main air compressors are usually two-stage with an intercooler because:
options: Cooling between stages cuts the work needed and keeps temperatures safe
It heats the air to the temperature required for starting
It reduces the air pressure to a safe level for the receiver
It removes the need for drains between the compressor stages and the receiver
explanation: Drains after each cooler remove condensed water and oil.

question: A dribbling (leaking) fuel injector nozzle causes:
options: Increased compression pressure and a faster rate of ignition
Poor combustion, nozzle carbon deposits and higher exhaust temperature
Better fuel economy, a cleaner exhaust and a lower exhaust gas temperature
Lower cylinder temperatures and a cleaner exhaust
explanation: Fuel that dribbles after the end of injection burns late and incompletely.

question: Using a high-BN cylinder oil with very low sulphur fuel for a long time can cause:
options: Lower cylinder oil consumption with no other effects on the engine
Hard calcium deposits on the piston crown, bore polishing and liner wear
Fuel pump seizure, because of a lack of lubrication of the plunger
Cold corrosion of the liner, caused by acid condensing at low temperature
explanation: The cylinder oil BN should be matched to the sulphur content of the fuel and the feed rate adjusted.

question: Cold corrosion of cylinder liners is caused by:
options: Sulphuric acid condensing on a liner below the acid dew point
High exhaust temperatures which burn the oil film on the liner
Sea water leaking into the scavenge space from the air cooler
Too much cylinder oil being fed to the liner by the lubricators
explanation: It is more likely at low load with high-sulphur fuel; jacket temperature and cylinder oil BN help control it.

question: When a distillate fuel such as MGO is used in an engine designed for HFO, a fuel cooler may be needed to:
options: Prevent wax from forming in the tank in cold weather
Raise the fuel's sulphur content to meet the requirements of the ECA rules
Keep the fuel viscosity above the minimum at the injection pumps
Increase the fuel's flash point to the level required by SOLAS
explanation: Very low viscosity increases internal leakage and the risk of fuel pump seizure; makers typically specify a minimum of about 2-3 cSt.

question: Engine makers commonly recommend that catalytic fines (Al + Si) in the fuel at the engine inlet be kept below about:
options: 150 mg/kg
60 mg/kg
500 mg/kg
15 mg/kg
explanation: ISO 8217 allows up to 60 mg/kg in the bunker; efficient centrifuging must reduce it before the engine.

question: Low compression pressure in one cylinder, with normal scavenge pressure, most likely indicates:
options: High jacket water temperature caused by a failed thermostat
Fuel injection timing which is too early for the load of the engine
A dirty turbocharger air filter which restricts the intake air
Leaking piston rings, a leaking exhaust valve or excessive liner wear
explanation: Compression pressure depends only on the air trapped and the sealing of the cylinder, not on fuel injection.

question: On many modern two-stroke engines, the exhaust valve is:
options: Opened by a rocker arm and closed by coil springs only
Opened by starting air
Opened hydraulically and closed by an air spring
Kept open permanently at sea
explanation: The air spring gives a reliable closing force with low wear; the valve also rotates to even out seat wear.

question: After an engine is stopped because of a high oil mist alarm, the crankcase doors should not be opened until:
options: The engine has cooled for enough time, typically 20 minutes or more
The engine has stopped turning and the turning gear has been engaged
The lube oil pump has been stopped for at least one minute
The scavenge drains have been opened and the air blowers stopped
explanation: Opening too soon can let in air and cause a crankcase explosion; keep people away from the relief valves.

question: Cylinder liner wear in a two-stroke engine is usually greatest:
options: At the bottom of the liner, near the scavenge ports of the cylinder
Near the top of the liner, at the top ring position at TDC
Evenly along the whole length of the liner surface
Around the scavenge ports only, where the ring edges pass
explanation: High temperature, pressure and poor lubrication near TDC cause the most wear; it is measured with a liner gauge at set positions.

question: Indicated power of a two-stroke cylinder depends on mean indicated pressure, piston area, stroke and:
options: Engine speed, as there is one power stroke per revolution
Half the engine speed, as there is one power stroke per two revolutions
The cooling water temperature at the outlet of the jacket
The sulphur content of the fuel which is burned in the cylinder
explanation: For a four-stroke engine the number of power strokes is half the revolutions.

question: According to the propeller law, if main engine speed is reduced by 10%, the power required falls to about:
options: 81% of the original (using speed squared)
90% of the original
50% of the original
73% of the original
explanation: Power is roughly proportional to the cube of speed: 0.9³ ≈ 0.73. This is why slow steaming saves so much fuel.

question: Variable Injection Timing (VIT) on a main engine is used to:
options: Control the speed of the turbocharger at part load
Advance injection at part load to keep high peak pressure and save fuel
Change the engine's direction of rotation by moving the cam
Delay the injection at all loads to reduce wear on the liner and rings
explanation: At high load the timing is retarded to stop the maximum pressure exceeding its limit.

question: The overspeed trip on a diesel generator engine typically operates at about:
options: 200% of rated speed (maximum)
150% of rated speed
110-115% of rated speed
90% of rated speed
explanation: It shuts off fuel to prevent damage from excessive centrifugal forces.

question: On a crosshead engine, the piston rod stuffing box:
options: Seals the stern tube from the sea water outside the hull of the ship
Holds the crosshead bearing to the piston rod of the engine
Seals the scavenge space from the crankcase and scrapes the piston rod
Seals the plunger of the fuel injection pump of the cylinder
explanation: Leaking stuffing boxes let cylinder oil and combustion residues contaminate the system oil.
